title: Your answers must match your N-400 form
description: The officer has your Form N-400 on the desk. They will read your answers back to you and ask you to say if they are correct. Keep a copy of your form and read it again before you go, so you remember what you wrote. If something has changed — a new job, a new address, a new trip, a new child — tell the officer. Changes are normal. Hiding a change is the problem.

title: The small talk is already part of the test
description: There is no special moment when the English speaking test begins. From the first “Good morning, how are you today?” the officer is already listening to your English. So answer in full sentences, not just “Yes” or “Fine.” Say “Good morning. I am well, thank you.” This is why the Mock Interview starts with greeting and small talk. Practice that part out loud too — do not skip it.

title: Answer only the question the officer asks
description: If the officer asks “Have you ever been arrested?”, answer that question. Do not tell a long story. Short, true, and complete is best. Extra details only lead to extra questions.

title: It is okay to ask the officer to repeat
description: If you do not understand, say: “I'm sorry, could you repeat that, please?” or “Could you say that a different way, please?” This is allowed, and officers hear it every day. It is much better than guessing at a question you did not hear.

title: Always tell the truth
description: You take an oath at the start of the interview. A wrong answer can be fixed. A lie cannot. Some “Yes” answers are not automatic problems — but hiding them is a serious problem. If you are worried about any answer on your form, talk to an immigration lawyer before your interview, not during it.

title: Practice out loud, not in your head
description: The officer scores how you speak. Reading quietly does not practice speaking. Say every answer out loud, even when you are alone. Record yourself on your phone and listen. You will hear what to fix.

title: Learn the idea, not just the sounds
description: Officers do not always use the same words as this book. “Who is the Commander in Chief?” and “Who is in charge of the military?” want the same answer: the President. If you understand the idea, you can answer any wording. If you only memorize sounds, one new word can stop you.

title: One correct answer is enough
description: Many answers give you several choices, separated by a semicolon (;). You do not need to say all of them. Pick the one that is easiest for you to remember and say, and use that same one every time.

title: A little every day beats a lot once a week
description: Fifteen minutes each day will teach you more than three hours on Sunday. Use the 8-Week Study Plan in the workbook to keep going at a steady speed.

title: Check the current officials before you go
description: Some answers change over time: the President, the Vice President, your state's U.S. Senators, your Representative, the Speaker of the House, the Chief Justice, and your Governor. Check them at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates a few days before your interview.

title: Bring these documents with you
description: Pack your folder the night before and check it again at the door.
items: All of your passports — current and expired
Your state ID or driver's license
Anything else your appointment notice asks you to bring (for example: marriage or divorce papers, tax records, or court papers)

title: Arrive early
description: Plan for traffic and for parking. Try to arrive 30 minutes before your appointment time. Arriving calm helps your English.

title: Turn your phone off
description: Do this before you go into the interview room, not after it rings.

title: Dress neatly
description: Dress the way you would for a job interview. You do not need a suit. Clean and tidy is enough.

title: Speak slowly and clearly
description: You do not need perfect English and you do not need to lose your accent. The officer needs to understand you — that is all. Slower is clearer.

title: If you do not pass everything the first time, you get a second chance
description: USCIS will test you again on only the part you did not pass. They schedule it 60 to 90 days after your first interview. So one hard day is not the end. Keep practicing.

title: Do not stay silent when you are confused
description: Silence looks like you did not understand the English. Asking the officer to repeat shows that you did.

title: Do not memorize words you do not understand
description: If you learn only the sound of an answer, you will lose it as soon as the officer changes one word in the question.

title: Do not forget your trips outside the United States
description: The officer will ask about your travel. Before you go, write down every trip using the stamps and dates in your passport. Guessing at dates in the interview looks careless.

title: Do not forget to report a new address
description: If you moved after you filed Form N-400, you must tell USCIS — usually within 10 days of moving, using Form AR-11. Do not wait for the interview to mention it.

title: Do not study only the civics questions
description: Many people pass civics and then struggle with reading, writing, or speaking. Give time to the Reading and Writing practice as well, and read your practice sentences out loud.

title: Do not rely on old answers you learned from a friend
description: Test versions and officeholders change. Use the test version that matches your N-400 filing date, and check uscis.gov/citizenship before your interview.

title: Remember: the officer is not trying to fail you
description: They ask these questions every day, and they want you to succeed. Prepare well, tell the truth, and speak up when you need help.
